[EMERGING] A soft robot that inches through the small intestine 🤖

MIT engineers and partners built a soft, tethered enteroscope that moves like an inchworm: balloons at its head and tail take turns anchoring while four-chamber actuators extend and bend the body. A kirigami-patterned skin adds grip. It carries a camera, a drug sprayer and clips for small biopsies or polyps. The work is published in Science Robotics.

Reality check: in animal tests it traveled about 6.5 feet. The small intestine is more than 20 feet long, and doctors need to evaluate a 20 to 25 foot segment. The team says navigation still needs work, and there is no timeline for human trials.

2:
[EMERGING] Robots that know when they're unsure

The analogy: you glimpse a coat on a chair in dim light and think it's a person. Robots that build 3D maps with vision-language AI make the same kind of mistake, and a wrong label can persist in their memory.

MIT's UQ-DAAAM system gives each label a single uncertainty score by combining how confident the AI is with how consistent the label is across viewpoints. When doubt is high, the robot picks extra views to re-check. MIT reports it resolved ambiguity for about 92% of objects, needing only two additional captions per object.

Caveat: the work is a preprint headed to the NeurIPS conference, not yet a peer-reviewed journal paper, and results come from test settings.

3:
[IMAGINE] What if machines grew stronger the more they worked? 💪

Today: MIT researchers built a paper-thin, gum-sized swimmer driven by genetically engineered living muscle on two fins. Shining light on one fin makes it contract, and switching the light steers the robot through a water maze. Its skeleton is a gel film half a millimeter thick, and its top speed is about four body lengths per minute.

Reality check: it was tested in a petri dish with the light aimed by hand. The researchers point to possible uses like environmental monitoring in water. Robots that train and strengthen like muscle are our speculation, not a result.

Where would you want a muscle-powered robot working? Tell us in the comments.

4:
[EMERGING] Back to the scene of an asteroid-deflection test 🛰️

ESA's Hera spacecraft has sent its first close-up of the Didymos asteroid pair, taken from 60 km away with its framing camera. It shows the side of Didymos that NASA's DART never imaged before it hit the small moon Dimorphos in 2022: boulders, craters and possible grooves or ridges.

Why it matters: DART's impact shortened Dimorphos's orbit by 33 minutes, far more than predicted. Hera is there to study the aftermath, starting with a close look at the impact area.

Caveat: ESA's team says the surface features may come from material thrown off Dimorphos, but that idea still has to be tested. Dimorphos was mostly in shadow. Detailed images of both asteroids are due Nov 25.

[TODAY] Why fire your engine when you're already going fastest?

The analogy: on a swing, a pump at the bottom of the arc, where you move fastest, adds the most energy. Rockets get the same bonus, called the Oberth effect: a burn at peak speed during a close planetary pass adds more energy than the same burn elsewhere.

NASA's twin ESCAPADE probes are using it now. Each swoops 600 to 1,100 miles above Earth and fires its engine for about 9 minutes, adding more than 1,000 mph and bending its path toward Mars. NASA says no Mars-bound spacecraft has flown a powered flyby like this before. Spacecraft 1 was scheduled for Nov 7; Spacecraft 2 follows on Monday, Nov 9.

Caveat: NASA checks the new trajectory several days after each burn and may make correction maneuvers. Arrival at Mars is planned for September 2027.

[IMAGINE] What if robotic tugs could keep great telescopes alive for decades? 🔭

Today: Hubble has no propulsion, so atmospheric drag is slowly lowering its orbit. NASA predicts reentry around 2033 to 2034. On Oct 29, NASA issued a request for information asking companies what they could offer: a boost to a higher orbit, servicing to improve its capabilities, or a controlled reentry. Responses are due Nov 30, and NASA says any mission would need to fly by 2032.

Reality check: this is information gathering only. There is no contract, no chosen company and no funded mission. Routine robotic servicing of observatories is our speculation.

Which space telescope would you rescue first, and why? Tell us in the comments.

[EMERGING] Writing magnetic memory with a beam of light ✨

UC San Diego engineers used shaped ultrafast laser light to switch and reconfigure magnetic domains, the tiny regions that store bits in magnetic memory. They did it in a stack of nine alternating platinum and cobalt layers; earlier experiments worked with no more than three. The switching also did not require a specific light polarization. The work is published in Nature Communications.

Reality check: the team says optical switching could be more than 1,000 times faster than using magnetic fields, but that is a projection, not a measured result. Ultrafast lasers are hard to build into chips, and the researchers note significant technical obstacles before everyday use.

8:
[EMERGING] How do you hide an object from a heat camera?

The analogy: a stream flows around a rock and closes up behind it, so downstream you can't tell the rock is there. Thermal cloaks do this with heat, using a material whose internal structure guides heat around an object.

Engineers at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign and the Technical University of Denmark built 3D cloaks from a 3D-printed aluminum lattice, which carries heat, filled with a rubber-like material that conducts it poorly. The lattice can be tuned separately in three directions. Under an infrared camera, it hid intricate 3D shapes. The work is published in Nature Communications.

Caveat: the cloak only hides heat coming from outside sources, not objects that generate their own. Uses such as managing heat in electronics are future possibilities.

[IMAGINE] What if rooftops went tandem? ☀️

Today: perovskite-silicon tandem solar cells stack two light-absorbing layers so one cell can capture more of the solar spectrum. In July, LONGi reported a tandem cell at 35.5% efficiency, certified by the European Solar Test Installation. That is above the 33.7% theoretical limit for single-junction cells. The company page puts the tandem limit at up to 43%.

Reality check: this is a company-reported lab record, though independently certified, and it is not a mass-production figure. The company's reported tandem modules are lower, at 31.4%. Whether tandems reach rooftops depends on durability and manufacturing, which is where our speculation begins.

What's the biggest hurdle for tandem solar on rooftops? Tell us in the comments.
